title: The Best Offer Currently Available in the Marketplace: What Citadel Securities Saw and What It Filled

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is a penny at a time and the Commission prices it. On settlement Citadel Securities paid "disgorgement of $5,200,000, prejudgment interest of $1,465,268, and a civil money penalty of $16,000,000". The disgorgement is the Commission's figure for what the conduct earned over roughly two years and 2.7 million retail orders — about two dollars an order.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is in the market's own architecture, and the order describes it without euphemism. The consolidated public feeds, the SIPs, "disseminate the best-priced, round lot quotations" and compute the National Best Bid and Offer; they "do not disseminate odd lot quotations". Direct exchange feeds carry "information about all displayed quotations, executions, and cancellations", from which "Market participants can use these depth of book feeds to construct their own view of the full displayed limit order book". Two pictures of the same market, one public and coarser, one private and finer, both lawful to hold.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is a sentence given to customers: CES described a market order to certain retail broker-dealer clients as an "[o]rder to buy (sell) at the best offer (bid) currently available in the marketplace". The Commission found that "These statements were materially misleading in light of the way FastFill and SmartProvide functioned. The statements suggested that CES would either internalize a marketable order at, or seek to obtain for that order through routing, the best price for that order that CES observed on the various market data feeds it referenced, which FastFill and SmartProvide did not do." The firm held the better picture and quoted the worse one.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is the gap between the two feeds, taken on one side only, and the Commission's own worked example is the clearest statement of it: "if CES was handling a marketable order to buy shares, and the SIP best offer was $10.01, and the best offer from one or more of the depth of book feeds was $10.00, FastFill immediately internalized the order using the SIP offer of $10.01 per share. FastFill did not internalize at or seek to obtain through routing the better $10.00 price from the depth of book feeds." The mirror-image algorithm, SmartProvide, ran when the public price was the better one; it did not fill at the public price either, and for some orders the result was "a price that was worse than they otherwise would have received in the absence of SmartProvide."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The settlement is the stage, and its terms are the standard ones. The respondent "submitted an Offer of Settlement" and consented "without admitting or denying the findings". The violation found is Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act — a negligence-based misstatement provision, not fraud with intent. The algorithms "CES has since discontinued". The sanctions are a cease-and-desist, a censure, and money. Nobody is named, nobody is barred, and the conduct ended seven years before the order issued.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Regulation NMS and the SIP architecture, and the payment-for-order-flow arrangement the order describes as routine: retail brokers send marketable orders to "internalizers", "OTC market makers", or "wholesale market makers", which "often make payments to the retail broker-dealers that send them these orders". The Commission's own 2010 Concept Release is quoted for the scale: "nearly 100% of their customer orders are routed to OTC market makers".
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Nothing structural in this order. What it creates is a precedent about disclosure rather than execution: the holding is that describing a market order as filled at "the best offer currently available in the marketplace" is materially misleading if the firm's own feeds show a better price it does not pursue. The two-tier feed itself is untouched.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Retail brokers route essentially all marketable orders to wholesalers and are paid for it; the wholesaler's advantage is the finer data picture; the finer picture is monetised against the coarser one the customer is quoted; and the resulting concentration makes the arrangement harder to leave — by the date of this order one firm's execution arm handled "approximately 35% of the average daily volume of retail equity shares traded in the U.S. markets".

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That high-frequency firms systematically front-run retail orders, and that Citadel and Jane Street were caught doing it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: JANE STREET IS NOT IN THIS DOCUMENT. The order concerns one respondent, Citadel Securities LLC, and the node's original title naming a second firm has been replaced, because nothing read supports it. Nor is the finding front-running. The Commission found a willful violation of Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act — a misstatement provision — on the ground that a written disclosure describing a market order as filled at "the best offer (bid) currently available in the marketplace" was materially misleading given how two algorithms actually behaved. There is no finding of trading ahead of customer orders, no finding of intent to defraud, no individual charged, and no admission: Citadel Securities settled "without admitting or denying the findings". The Commission's own figures also cut the scale down hard, and this dossier reports them: FastFill and SmartProvide "handled a small portion of CES's overall order flow, approximately 2.6% of the retail orders handled by CES's algorithmic trading engine and 0.6% of CES's overall order flow", and for about 18% of the shares SmartProvide handled the customer got a better price than the public quote. The conduct ran from late 2007 to January 2010 and the algorithms were discontinued. WHAT SURVIVES ALL OF THAT is the thing the legend gets right in substance and wrong in mechanism: the advantage was the data, not the queue. The firm subscribed to depth-of-book feeds that showed prices the consolidated public feed did not, and the Commission found that when those feeds showed a better price, FastFill "did not internalize at or seek to obtain through routing the better $10.00 price" — it filled at the public $10.01 and kept the difference. The asymmetry was lawful to hold; what was sanctioned was telling the customer it did not exist.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A settled SEC order of 13 January 2017, In the Matter of Citadel Securities LLC, Securities Act Release No. 10280, Exchange Act Release No. 79790, Admin. Proc. File No. 3-17772. It finds: that from late 2007 through January 2010, Citadel Execution Services received both the consolidated public SIP feeds and direct exchange depth-of-book feeds; that two algorithms, FastFill and SmartProvide, were triggered by differences between them; that FastFill internalized marketable orders at the SIP price or better even when a depth-of-book feed showed a better price, without pursuing that better price; that SmartProvide, when the SIP price was better, routed a non-marketable order displayed for one to five seconds instead, improving on the public quote for about 18% of shares handled and leaving some internalized orders worse off than without it; that CES gave certain retail broker-dealer clients a written disclosure describing a market order as an order to buy or sell at the best offer or bid currently available in the marketplace; that these statements were materially misleading in light of how the algorithms functioned; and that Citadel Securities willfully violated Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act. It records FastFill as having executed approximately 2.7 million retail orders between June 2008 and January 2010, roughly 20% of FastFill internalizations triggered by odd-lot quotations, the two algorithms as about 2.6% of the algorithmic engine's retail orders and 0.6% of overall order flow, approximately 70 broker-dealer clients and 1.2 million orders a day in the relevant period against approximately 200 clients and 2.9 million orders a day by 2017 — about 35% of average daily US retail equity share volume — and the algorithms as discontinued. Sanctions: cease and desist, censure, disgorgement of $5,200,000, prejudgment interest of $1,465,268 and a civil money penalty of $16,000,000, on a settlement without admission or denial.

citations.title: In the Matter of Citadel Securities LLC, Securities and Exchange Commission, Order Instituting Administrative and Cease-and-Desist Proceedings, Securities Act Release No. 10280 / Exchange Act Release No. 79790, Administrative Proceeding File No. 3-17772, 13 January 2017
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov refuses a generic browser user-agent and serves the file to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) THIS IS A SETTLED ORDER: the respondent "submitted an Offer of Settlement" and consented "without admitting or denying the findings here, except as to the Commission's jurisdiction". THE SUBJECT IS THE LATENCY GAP ITSELF, described by the Commission in plain terms. During "late 2007 through January 2010", Citadel Execution Services received market data from "(1) the consolidated public feeds (known as 'SIP' feeds ...) and (2) several data feeds sent directly by individual stock exchanges (known as 'direct feeds')". The SIPs "disseminate the best-priced, round lot quotations ... and calculate and identify the National Best Bid ... and National Best Offer", and "do not disseminate odd lot quotations". The direct feeds are "depth of book" feeds carrying "information about all displayed quotations, executions, and cancellations on the relevant exchange", from which "Market participants can use these depth of book feeds to construct their own view of the full displayed limit order book". TWO ALGORITHMS, AND WHAT EACH DID. "One strategy, known as FastFill, was triggered when the best price from one or more of the depth of book feeds that FastFill referenced was better than the best price disseminated by the SIP feed. Assuming all other eligibility conditions were met, FastFill immediately internalized a marketable order at the SIP NBB or NBO, as applicable, or better." The Commission's own worked example: "if CES was handling a marketable order to buy shares, and the SIP best offer was $10.01, and the best offer from one or more of the depth of book feeds was $10.00, FastFill immediately internalized the order using the SIP offer of $10.01 per share. FastFill did not internalize at or seek to obtain through routing the better $10.00 price from the depth of book feeds." The second, SmartProvide, was triggered when the SIP price was better than the depth-of-book price, and instead of filling at the SIP price it "would route a non-marketable order to the market" displayed "for up to one to five seconds". That worked for some customers — "This occurred for approximately 18% of the shares handled by SmartProvide" — and against others: "Some of the orders that CES internalized after SmartProvide displayed an order in the market on their behalf received a price that was worse than they otherwise would have received in the absence of SmartProvide." WHAT THE CUSTOMERS HAD BEEN TOLD: CES gave certain retail broker-dealer clients a written disclosure describing a market order as an "[o]rder to buy (sell) at the best offer (bid) currently available in the marketplace". The Commission found: "These statements were materially misleading in light of the way FastFill and SmartProvide functioned. The statements suggested that CES would either internalize a marketable order at, or seek to obtain for that order through routing, the best price for that order that CES observed on the various market data feeds it referenced, which FastFill and SmartProvide did not do." "As a result of its conduct, Citadel Securities willfully violated Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act." SCALE, AND THE COMMISSION'S OWN LIMITING FIGURES. In the relevant period CES had "approximately 70 broker-dealer clients" and received about 1.2 million equity orders a day, around 2.3 billion shares; "FastFill executed approximately 2.7 million retail orders between June 2008 and January 2010"; and the two algorithms together "handled a small portion of CES's overall order flow, approximately 2.6% of the retail orders handled by CES's algorithmic trading engine and 0.6% of CES's overall order flow". For about 20% of orders internalized by FastFill, "the triggering event was caused by an odd" lot quotation. As of the order's date CES had "approximately 200 broker-dealer clients", received about 2.9 million orders a day, and its processing "accounts on average for approximately 35% of the average daily volume of retail equity shares traded in the U.S. markets". SANCTIONS: cease and desist; "Respondent is censured"; and payment within 14 days of "disgorgement of $5,200,000, prejudgment interest of $1,465,268, and a civil money penalty of $16,000,000". The order also records that the two algorithms were discontinued. WHAT IS NOT IN THIS DOCUMENT: Jane Street is not mentioned anywhere in it, and neither is any other firm as a respondent. There is no finding of front-running, no finding that any individual acted with intent to defraud, no criminal referral, and no admission of the findings.
